videoIdeas.title: The 3 networking questions that actually work
videoIdeas.hook: Stop asking people 'so what do you do?' — it's the fastest way to be forgotten.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart01 pulled 976k views on an authentic-networking-questions video, and lifeofdinoo_ got 92 comments on a communication post. Practical, list-style 'exact words to say' content is the single biggest format working in this niche right now, and I have nothing like it on my grid.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop asking people 'so what do you do?' — it's the fastest way to be forgotten.

Everyone asks that. Which means your conversation sounds like everyone else's. Here's three questions that actually make people remember you.

One: 'What's something you're working on that you're actually excited about?' You get energy, not a job title.

Two: 'How did you end up doing this?' People love telling their story. Let them.

Three, and this is the one nobody uses: 'Who should I be talking to that you know?' That's how a conversation becomes an introduction.

Networking isn't about collecting people. It's about being the one worth remembering. Ask better, and you won't have to chase.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-frame, somewhere clean and slightly busy — a university corridor, a co-working space, or outside an event. Smart casual. Calm, direct energy, talking straight to camera like you're pulling someone aside.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'so what do you do?' with a big red cross slashing through it as you say the line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-walk through an event space, turning to camera as you deliver the first line
On-screen counter '3 questions' ticking up in the corner so people stay for all three
Pattern interrupt: start by miming a limp, boring handshake then cut to you talking

videoIdeas.title: 5 'leadership' habits that are actually just insecurity
videoIdeas.hook: Half the things people call leadership are just a fear of being disliked.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's '5 careers I don't want' (161k views) and '5 specialties I love' prove the numbered contrarian-list format is dominating. A blunt 'what you think is leadership isn't' angle fits my voice and fills a gap — my leadership pillar is barely represented on the grid.
videoIdeas.script:
Half the things people call leadership are just a fear of being disliked.

One: saying yes to everything. That's not dedication. That's not being able to hold a boundary.

Two: doing everyone's job for them. You're not helping. You're telling your team you don't trust them.

Three: never showing you're wrong. A leader who can't say 'I messed that up' makes everyone else hide their mistakes too.

Four: being the loudest in every room. Volume isn't authority. The person everyone goes quiet for usually speaks the least.

Five: needing to be liked. The moment being liked matters more than being respected, you've stopped leading.

Real leadership is boring. It's boundaries, ownership, and being okay with people being annoyed at you. That's it.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing in a plain, slightly moody setting — dark shirt, simple background. Low, steady energy. You're not performing, you're telling someone the truth they didn't want.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text counter '1 of 5' with each insecurity typed out and then struck through as you reframe it.
otherHookIdeas: Open on the punchline reframe ('needing to be liked') then cut back to 'let me explain'
Hold up five fingers and drop one per point as a visual progress bar
On-screen text punchline that contradicts the common belief, e.g. 'saying yes = weak'

videoIdeas.title: Why your voice shakes when you speak (and the fix)
videoIdeas.hook: Your voice doesn't shake because you're nervous. It shakes because you're rushing.
videoIdeas.rationale: saffanabanana's whiteboard 'media literacy' explainer hit 29k and lifeofdinoo_ built a whole DM funnel around communication. Tactical public-speaking breakdowns perform, and this solves a problem every young Muslim feels at talks, halaqas, and interviews. Public speaking is a named pillar I underuse.
videoIdeas.script:
Your voice doesn't shake because you're nervous. It shakes because you're rushing.

When you're scared, you speed up to get it over with. Fast breathing, no pauses, and your voice has nothing to stand on. So it trembles.

The fix isn't confidence. You can't summon that on command. The fix is pace.

Before you speak, breathe out fully — not in, out. Empty lungs force you to slow down. Then say your first sentence slower than feels normal. Painfully slow.

Then use the pause. Silence feels like death to you and like control to everyone watching. The person who can sit in a three-second pause owns the room.

You don't need to feel calm. You need to move like you are. The feeling catches up.

visuals.setting: Close-ish framing, calm room, soft light. Neutral top. Deliberately slow delivery that demonstrates the advice as you give it — practice what you preach on camera.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'it's not nerves →' appearing over a close-up as you deliver the corrective first line.
otherHookIdeas: Demonstrate: say one sentence fast and shaky, then repeat it slow and steady, hard cut between the two
On-screen waveform/audio visual that steadies as you slow down
Cold open holding a long silent pause looking at camera before the first word

videoIdeas.title: The gym taught me more about discipline than any book
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest runner in any room. I just keep showing up to the room.
videoIdeas.rationale: My single best post is the running one — 880 views, 110 likes, 10 comments — far above my average. The audience responds to me being honest about effort over talent. Doubling down on that proven personal-discipline angle, tied to my actual running, is the clearest signal in my own data.
videoIdeas.script:
I'm not the fastest runner in any room. I just keep showing up to the room.

For a long time I thought discipline was about motivation. Feeling ready. Being in the mood. Then I started running, and running does not care about your mood.

Some mornings I'm slow. Some mornings everyone passes me. But the version of me that laced up on the bad days is the one that's still here months later.

That's the whole secret people overcomplicate. You're not competing with the fastest person. You're competing with the version of you that wanted to stay in bed.

Talent sets your ceiling. Showing up on the days you don't want to decides whether you ever reach it.

Stop trying to be the best in the room. Just refuse to be the one who left.

visuals.setting: Shot outdoors mid or post-run — athletic wear, slightly out of breath, park or path at golden hour. Raw and real, not polished. Energy is grounded and a bit tired, which sells the authenticity.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, breathing audible, then you slow to a stop and turn to camera for the first line.
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text 'not the fastest' over footage of other runners passing you
Open on lacing up shoes in the dark/early morning as a visual metaphor
Hard cut from an empty bed to you already running — the choice visualised

videoIdeas.title: What history's conquerors knew about winning hearts
videoIdeas.hook: In 711 AD people begged a Muslim army to invade them. Think about what that takes.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post pulled 437 views — my second best — showing my audience responds to Islamic history framed as leadership lessons. Nobody in my competitor set is reliably mining history for leadership content; it's a genuine differentiator in my voice.
videoIdeas.script:
In 711 AD people begged a Muslim army to invade them. Think about what that takes.

Tariq bin Ziyad crossed into Spain and the oppressed didn't resist him — they welcomed him. That's not military strength. You don't get welcomed by force.

Here's the leadership lesson everyone misses. People don't follow the most powerful person. They follow the person who makes their situation better than the one they're trapped in.

Andalusia wasn't built on conquest alone. It was built on justice being more attractive than the tyranny people were living under.

Apply that to anything. A team, a cause, a room. You don't win people by overpowering them. You win them by being the better option so clearly that choosing you is obvious.

Authority that's taken fades. Authority that's welcomed lasts centuries.

visuals.setting: Indoors, warmer tone, simple and considered — collared top, plain backdrop. Measured, storyteller energy. You're teaching, not hyping.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '711 AD' bold over a dark frame as you open with the date, like a documentary cold open.
otherHookIdeas: Open on a map of the Strait of Gibraltar then cut to your face for the lesson
On-screen text posing the question 'why would people WANT to be invaded?'
Lower-third captions styled like a history doc to signal 'this is a real story'

videoIdeas.title: Burnout isn't weakness — it's a signal you ignored
videoIdeas.hook: Burnout isn't you being weak. It's your body sending invoices you refused to pay.
videoIdeas.rationale: My Sabr/burnout post (209 views) and doctordaanish's journaling video (24k views, 3.8k likes) both show mental-health-for-high-performers content lands hard right now. Reframing burnout bluntly — not softly — is on-brand and separates me from the gentle wellness accounts.
videoIdeas.script:
Burnout isn't you being weak. It's your body sending invoices you refused to pay.

We treat it like it appears out of nowhere. It doesn't. It builds. The skipped sleep, the no breaks, the 'I'll rest after this deadline' that you've said eleven times.

And the people most at risk aren't the lazy ones. It's the students, the medics, the ones who care too much to stop. Caring isn't a shield against burnout. It's the fuel for it.

The fix isn't a weekend off. It's catching the early signs — the irritability, the dread, the small habits slipping — before they become a wall you can't climb.

Rest isn't the reward for finishing. It's part of the work. Build the small habits now, or your body will force the big break later. Your choice which.

visuals.setting: Calm, lower-lit room, relaxed but direct. Plain top. Slower, almost confessional energy — you're leveling with someone who's running on empty.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'burnout ≠ weakness' appearing as you say the reframed opening line.
otherHookIdeas: Open on a phone screen full of notifications/deadlines then cut to your face
On-screen text listing the ignored early signs one by one as a checklist
Pattern interrupt: start by closing a laptop slowly and exhaling before speaking

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post by a mile — 880 views, 110 likes, 10 comments. The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its purest: short, blunt, quietly confident, and universally relatable. Effort-over-talent framing clearly resonates with your audience.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left value on the table by stopping at the one-liner. Add a second line that turns the aphorism into a takeaway people can save or tag someone with, and pin a comment that asks 'what room are you refusing to leave?' to convert those 110 likes into more comments and shares.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your second-strongest post (437 views). Islamic history as a leadership lesson is a genuine differentiator — none of your competitors do this consistently, and the strong hook date '711 AD' does documentary-style work before you even speak.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite decent views means it informed but didn't provoke. The caption gets cut off mid-sentence ('Andalusia wasn't built t...') — front-load the actual lesson into the first caption line and end with a direct question like 'would people welcome your leadership, or just tolerate it?' to pull replies.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Never running through a park at night ever again 😭' is a great example of a casual, human, funny caption — 45 likes and 5 comments on 372 views is a healthy engagement rate. It shows personality and makes you approachable, not just instructional.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This is pure moment with no takeaway, so it can't travel beyond people who already know you. Tie the relatable moment to one of your pillars — even a single line connecting the fear/discomfort to mindset or discipline — so a lighthearted clip still earns a save instead of just a laugh.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Tackling burnout is timely and on-pillar — doctordaanish's journaling video proves mental-health-for-high-performers content performs huge right now. Naming a specific audience ('whether you're a medical student or not') is a smart inclusivity move.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 209 views and 2 comments suggest it read as a product promo for Sabr rather than value-first content. The caption leads into the app too fast. Lead with the blunt insight about burnout, deliver the lesson, and only mention the tool at the very end — people share advice, they scroll past ads.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count here — proves your audience rallies hard behind justice-driven, values-led content, and anchoring it with the hadith gives it weight and shareability that matches your sharp-older-brother voice.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 1 comment against 289 likes means it generated agreement but not conversation, and as a Sidecar it missed the video reach every top post in your niche is getting. Reformat this kind of message as a direct-to-camera video with a clear ask ('say his name in the comments'), so the emotional energy converts into reach and replies, not just silent likes.
